methodological_rigor.justification: The MR design has serious weaknesses. The oral cavity cancer GWAS includes only 357 cases against 372,016 controls, which severely limits power and inflates the risk of unstable estimates and winner's curse. The instrumental-variable threshold (P<1×10⁻⁵) is relaxed well below genome-wide significance (5×10⁻⁸), and the manuscript's description of 'statistical significance P<5×10⁻⁶' is inconsistent with the IV criterion stated in Methods. The reported ORs (0.9993; 95% CI 0.9988–0.9997) are so close to the null that any interpretation of 'protective' causality is clinically implausible and may reflect residual pleiotropy or scale artifact rather than biology. MVMR is used but formal mediation analysis (e.g., Baron–Kenny or two-step MR with product/difference methods and bootstrap CIs) is not performed, and the authors concede this; yet mediation language is retained throughout. The in vitro work uses only two cell lines, no in vivo validation, and does not independently measure the HbA1c→immune-cell axis the MR describes.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: Two-sample MR studies are typically mapped to the level of individual cohort/genetic-epidemiology evidence (2b). The research question — glycemic control and oral cavity cancer — is clinically important, but the reported effect size (OR≈0.9993) is numerically indistinguishable from unity and offers no actionable clinical signal. The paradoxical direction (genetically higher HbA1c appearing 'protective' while AGEs impair CD8+ T-cell cytotoxicity in vitro) undermines any direct translational message about glycemic management for oral cancer prevention. The authors themselves acknowledge the ORs 'close to unity' lack clinical meaning, which severely tempers translational relevance.

reporting_quality.justification: The authors explicitly cite STROBE-MR adherence, which is the appropriate standard for MR studies (closest among listed options, hence 'other' given STROBE-MR is not listed; STROBE would be the parent framework). Key STROBE-MR items are partially covered: data sources, IV assumptions, sensitivity analyses (Cochran's Q, I², MR-Egger, leave-one-out), and reverse MR are described. However, population characteristics (ancestry overlap between HbA1c and outcome GWAS, sex distribution), full pre-specification, formal mediation framework, and conflict-of-interest/pre-registration are not reported. No explicit data/code availability statement is present; while source GWAS references are cited, the analysis code and intermediate IV lists are not deposited in named repositories, giving a weak reproducibility posture.

novelty_literature.justification: The paper claims the first MR of HbA1c on oral cavity cancer with immune-cell mediation, and that specific pairing is novel. However, the methodological template — two-sample MR with 731 immune-cell traits plus MVMR mediation plus modest in vitro validation — is now a highly saturated genre in 2023–2025 MR literature across many cancers (colorectal, pancreatic, HCC, head and neck broadly). Prior MR work on HbA1c and cancer in UK Biobank (Peila & Rohan, cited as ref 13) and head-and-neck cholesterol MR (Gormley et al., ref 17) already occupy adjacent space. The in vitro AGE/CD8+ T-cell oxidative-stress axis also replicates established mechanisms. Novelty is incremental rather than conceptual or paradigm-shifting.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is generally readable with a conventional structure, abstract that reflects the body, and informative figure captions. However, several passages are confusing or numerically dubious: the Methods state '7,723,107 SNPs were identified as the definitive instrumental variables relevant to oral cavity cancer,' which is implausibly large and left unexplained; the IV significance threshold is reported inconsistently (P<1×10⁻⁵ in Methods vs P<5×10⁻⁶ in Statistical Analysis). The Discussion is overlong, hedges extensively around the paradox between MR and in vitro directions, and relies on rhetorical bridges ('temporal windows,' 'immune compensation') that are not supported by data. Acronyms (OSCC, AGE, PBMC) are introduced appropriately but some sentences are awkward ('showcased considerable variation').

key_strengths: Combines two-sample MR with complementary in vitro functional assays (CCK-8, flow cytometry, LDH cytotoxicity, ROS measurement) addressing a clinically meaningful question
Appropriate standard sensitivity analyses reported (Cochran's Q, I², MR-Egger intercept, leave-one-out, Steiger directionality)
Explicit acknowledgement that effect sizes are close to unity and that MVMR does not formally establish mediation
key_concerns: Oral cavity cancer GWAS has only 357 cases, severely limiting power; the OR of 0.9993 is numerically indistinguishable from the null and clinically meaningless, yet is interpreted as 'protective'

IV p-value threshold set at P<1×10⁻⁵ (not genome-wide significant) with an internally inconsistent secondary threshold of P<5×10⁻⁶; implausible SNP counts (e.g., 7,723,107 'definitive instrumental variables') raise concern about Methods accuracy
Direction of MR estimate (protective) directly contradicts the in vitro finding that AGEs impair CD8+ T-cell cytotoxicity; the reconciliation offered in Discussion is speculative
No formal mediation analysis (two-step MR with proper indirect-effect estimation and bootstrap CIs); mediation language used despite the authors conceding this limitation
No explicit data/code availability statement; analysis code not deposited; limits reproducibility
In vitro work restricted to two OSCC cell lines with no in vivo validation and no direct test that HbA1c-associated AGE exposure levels are physiologic
chief_reviewer.rationale: The combination of near-null effect sizes, contradictory MR vs. experimental directions, loose IV thresholds, tiny case count, and absence of formal mediation analysis places this work in the lowest tier at best, and only with major revisions to the statistical framing, mediation methodology, and reconciliation of discordant findings.
